This shift toward a growth mindset and self-directed learning not only benefits the individual but also strengthens the overall resilience and performance of the team.
questions: Would you describe yourself as a self-directed learner?
Would you describe other people on your team as self-directed learners?
Do you believe that a growth mindset can be developed? Why or why not?

coaching.idea: A growth mindset supports taking responsibility for learning.
coaching.sampleResponse: I struggled with presentations, so I asked for feedback and practiced short briefings. Instead of saying I was simply bad at speaking, I tracked one skill to improve each week.
followUps: What did the person do independently to advance their learning?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: A growth mindset is not optimism alone or blaming every difficulty on insufficient effort.

reading: Learning prepares people for more responsibility. As people routinely put new knowledge and skills to work, they develop self-efficacy. Self- efficacy is a person’s belief in his or her ability to solve problems, overcome challenges, and complete individual tasks successfully.
example: For example, a team member can lead a small portion of a larger project after successfully completing training in project management. As they apply what they’ve learned – organizing tasks, coordinating with others, and solving issues as they arise – they begin to see the results of their efforts. Each success, no matter how small, reinforces their confidence in their abilities. The leader provides support and feedback along the way, gradually increasing the team member’s level of responsibility. As their self-efficacy grows, so does their motivation and willingness to take on bigger challenges – contributing to both their personal growth and the team’s strength as a whole.
questions: Would you rate your self-efficacy as high or low? Can your self-efficacy improve?
How would you rate the self-efficacy of others on your team?
Based on your experience, what are some other challenges and best practices for encouraging individual learning?

coaching.idea: Self-efficacy develops through successfully applying knowledge and skills.
coaching.sampleResponse: After several supported equipment checks, a trainee completed one independently and explained their decisions. Their confidence grew from demonstrated capability, so we gradually expanded their responsibility.
followUps: What evidence supports their confidence on this particular task?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Self-efficacy is task-related belief in capability, not general self-worth or confidence without competence.

tasks.title: Delegate Responsibility
tasks.what: Giving meaningful ownership of tasks and responsibilities.
tasks.why: Builds confidence, capability, and future leaders.

reading: Responsibility is a duty or task a person is required or expected to perform and be held accountable for. Delegating responsibility to team members provides opportunities for autonomy, ownership, and growth. Aspiring leaders will seek out opportunities for more responsibility. Delegating responsibility helps provide purpose.
example: For example, a leader assigns a team member responsible for coordinating a key client meeting, including setting the agenda, managing logistics, and leading the discussion. Although the task stretches the team member beyond their usual role, the leader expresses confidence in their ability and offers support as needed. The team member takes ownership of the task, prepares thoroughly, and successfully leads the meeting. Afterward, they reflect on what they learned and feel a strong sense of accomplishment. This experience not only builds their skills and confidence but also strengthens their connection to the team’s goals. By delegating meaningful responsibility, the leader helps the team member find greater purpose in their work.
questions: Do you frequently seek opportunities for more responsibility at work? Why or why not?
Do people on your team seek or avoid opportunities for more responsibility?

coaching.idea: Delegation gives meaningful ownership and opportunities to develop.
coaching.sampleResponse: I delegated the weekly stock review, explained the required outcome, and agreed on checkpoints. The employee chose the method and brought issues to me instead of waiting for step-by-step orders.
followUps: What did the person genuinely own?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Assigning chores while retaining every choice may offer little autonomy or growth.

reading: Delegating responsibility allows leaders to maximize their productivity. Leaders often have difficulty “letting go” of responsibilities that should be delegated.
example: For example, a leader used to managing every detail of a project realizes they are becoming overwhelmed and unable to focus on strategic priorities. After identifying tasks that others on the team can handle, the leader delegates the responsibility of managing the project timeline to a team member with strong organizational skills. At first, the leader feels hesitant to step back but soon sees that the team member is not only capable but thrives with the added responsibility. As a result, the leader has more time to focus on higher-level goals, and the team member gains confidence and a stronger sense of purpose. This shift improves the leader’s productivity and engagement with the team.
questions: How would you rate yourself at delegating responsibility? Could you improve?
Have you worked for someone reluctant to delegate responsibility?
In your experience, how does delegating responsibility affect motivation and commitment?
Based on your experience, what are some other challenges and best practices for delegating responsibility?

coaching.idea: Letting go of suitable responsibilities develops others and frees leader capacity.
coaching.sampleResponse: I handed routine scheduling to a trained colleague and reviewed exceptions weekly. That gave them practice and allowed me to address staffing forecasts without redoing their schedule each day.
followUps: What made you comfortable letting go, and what did you still monitor?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Delegation is neither abandoning oversight nor delegating a task and secretly doing it again yourself.

tasks.title: Empower Decision Making
tasks.what: Giving authority consistent with responsibility.

reading: Team members should be empowered to make decisions consistent with their responsibilities. Empower implies giving the means and official authority to do something. Decision-making is the cognitive process of gathering information, assessing alternatives, and selecting choices or courses of action. Leaders should expect people to make some bad decisions. Learning from mistakes is essential for personal and professional growth. Empowering decision-making helps provide purpose.
example: For example, a leader empowers a team member to make decisions about how to allocate resources for a small-scale marketing campaign. The team member researches options, weighs the pros and cons, and makes a decision that ultimately doesn’t produce the expected results. Instead of stepping in with criticism, the leader helps the team member analyze what went wrong and what could be done differently next time. The team member gains valuable insight and feels trusted and supported, even in failure. Over time, this empowerment builds confidence, encourages initiative, and reinforces the idea that their contributions matter – deepening their sense of purpose and commitment to the team.
questions: Is your authority to make decisions consistent with your responsibilities?
How would you rate yourself at empowering decision-making?
Have you ever worked for someone that was reluctant to empower decision-making?
In your experience, how does empowering decision-making affect motivation and commitment?

coaching.idea: Authority and resources should match a person's assigned responsibility.
listenFor: Support for learning from reasonable mistakes
coaching.sampleResponse: I made a team lead responsible for minor service recovery and authorized adjustments within a set limit. After an imperfect choice, we reviewed the reasoning and improved the guidance.
followUps: What could they decide without asking you, and when should they escalate?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Responsibility without matching authority is not empowerment; authority still needs boundaries.

reading: Leaders should encourage team members to make timely decisions. The desire for more information to make decisions must be balanced against timeliness. The willingness of team members to make decisions during times of adversity is critical.
example: For example, during a system outage affecting customer service, a team member is faced with deciding whether to implement a temporary workaround or wait for further technical input. Remembering their leader’s guidance about timely decision-making, they choose to move forward with the workaround to minimize disruption. Later, when the issue is resolved, the leader praises the team member for taking initiative and making a timely call under pressure. Even though the decision wasn’t perfect, it kept operations moving and demonstrated the team’s ability to respond in real time. Encouraging timely decision-making in moments like this builds confidence, reinforces purpose, and strengthens the team’s ability to navigate adversity together.
questions: How would you rate yourself at making timely decisions? Could you improve?
How would you rate yourself at making decisions under pressure? Could you improve?
Have you worked for someone who was not able to make timely decisions or decisions under pressure?
Based on your experience, what are some other challenges and best practices for empowering decision-making?

coaching.idea: Timely decisions balance useful information against the cost of waiting.
listenFor: A decision deadline and available evidence
A proportionate way to manage uncertainty
coaching.sampleResponse: We could not wait for perfect staffing forecasts. I asked the coordinator to choose coverage using current demand and a backup plan, then revisit it when new information arrived.
followUps: What information was essential, and what was merely nice to have?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Timely decision-making is not guessing blindly or skipping necessary safety checks.

tasks.title: Train the Team
tasks.what: Continuous development through on-the-job and formal training.

reading: Team training is an iterative process as teams work together over time. On-the-job team training is situated in real experience and should be continuous. Constructive feedback from leaders and team members is essential and should become a habit. Regularly scheduled formal team training should augment on-the-job training. Training the team helps develop cohesion.
example: For example, a marketing team working on multiple campaigns takes time each week to learn from one another by sharing updates on their work, explaining strategies they’ve used, and offering tips or tools that have been effective. This ongoing exchange of knowledge helps everyone stay aligned and continuously improve. To complement this peer learning, the team also attends quarterly training sessions on project management, creative thinking, and cross-functional collaboration. The combination of learning together through shared experience and formal training builds trust, encourages open communication, and strengthens cohesion within the team.
questions: Does your team see every day as an opportunity to improve their knowledge and skills?
Does your team welcome constructive feedback?
How often does your team participate in structured training events? Are those training events mostly effective or mostly not effective? Why?

coaching.idea: Team training combines repeated real-work practice with feedback and formal learning.
coaching.sampleResponse: After a handoff workshop, we practiced the routine on each shift and discussed missed details at the end. The next drill used those lessons rather than repeating the class unchanged.
followUps: How did formal instruction and everyday practice reinforce each other?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: A one-time course does not replace continuous team practice and constructive feedback.

reading: As teams successfully learn new knowledge and skills together, they develop social cohesion, task cohesion, and collective efficacy. Collective efficacy is the belief that a group can meet challenges and complete tasks together successfully. Teams that have collective efficacy are better prepared to overcome adversity together.
example: For example, after months of working together on a complex system upgrade, a technology team successfully launches the new platform with minimal issues. Throughout the project, they collaborated closely, solved problems, and supported one another during setbacks. As a result, they not only improved their technical skills but also built strong relationships and confidence in their ability to handle future challenges. When a new high-stakes project is announced, the team approaches it with a shared sense of optimism and determination. Their past success has strengthened their belief in each other and the team’s overall capability – this is collective efficacy in action, and it plays a key role in their continued cohesion and resilience.
questions: Does your team routinely learn new collective knowledge and skills together on the job?
How would you rate your team’s collective efficacy? Can it improve?
In your experience, how does training the team affect teamwork?
Based on your experience, what are some other challenges and best practices for training the team?

coaching.idea: Successful joint practice builds shared confidence and coordination.
coaching.sampleResponse: After several emergency drills, team members knew their roles and trusted the handoffs. In the next disruption, they coordinated more confidently because they had solved similar challenges together.
followUps: What could the group do together that supports its confidence?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Collective efficacy is belief in the team's joint capability, not simply adding up individual confidence.

modules.title: Team Learning
modules.theme: Teams learn from experience: Experiencing → Reflecting → Deciding → Acting. Single-loop improves the process; double-loop changes the assumptions.
glossary: Ambitious goals that pull performance up
Safe to speak honestly without punishment

tasks.title: Analyze Team Learning Capacity
tasks.what: Team learning is a continuous cycle of Experiencing → Reflecting → Deciding → Acting.
tasks.why: Teams learn from experience to improve, innovate, and solve problems.

reading: Team learning is the cyclical process of experiencing, reflecting, deciding, and acting as a team. Working together, teams learn from their experience how to improve, innovate, and solve problems. The experiential learning cycle is continuous in the workplace. Learning from their experience is how resilient teams overcome adversity and then adapt and grow together because of that adversity.
example: For example, after a project deadline is missed due to miscommunication, a resilient team debriefs to reflect on what went wrong and why. Through open discussion, they identify gaps in their planning and decision-making processes. Together, they decide on new communication protocols and project management tools to prevent similar issues in the future. As they implement these changes on their next project, they actively monitor outcomes and adjust as needed. This cycle of learning and adapting not only improves performance but also strengthens the team’s confidence in facing future challenges.
questions: Has your team recently solved a problem?
Has your team recently developed an innovation?
Has your team recently developed a new idea for improvement?

coaching.idea: Team learning is a repeating cycle of experience, reflection, decision, and action.
listenFor: A changed action followed by another experience
coaching.sampleResponse: We missed a delivery, reviewed the handoff, chose a shared checklist, and used it on the next run. We then reviewed that result to see whether the change helped.
followUps: Where did the team move from talking about the experience to doing something differently?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Reflection alone is not the full learning cycle, and a poor outcome can still generate learning.

reading: The experiencing stage of the experiential learning cycle is where teams directly observe or participate in events. Everything that a team does together creates an experience that can be learned from. Improving, innovating, and solving problems require teams to move from experiencing to reflecting. Teams that cannot move from experiencing to reflecting are not learning.
example: For example, a customer service team consistently receives complaints about long response times. Despite the persistent pattern, some senior team members dismissed the issue, arguing that the current process has “always worked” and that customers must be more patient. During team meetings, when others try to raise concerns or suggest improvements, these resistant members shut down the conversation or redirect it to other topics. As a result, the team fails to move from experiencing to reflecting. Without that reflection, no decisions for change are made, and the team misses the opportunity to learn from the experience and improve.
questions: Would you say teams can learn from their successes, failures, and everything else? Why or why not?
Based on your experience, what are some of the challenges that prevent teams from moving from experiencing to reflecting? How can those challenges be overcome?

coaching.idea: Experience becomes useful learning when teams examine it together.
listenFor: A success or failure used as evidence
A barrier to reflection and how it was addressed
coaching.sampleResponse: Our team kept repeating a slow setup without discussing it. We reserved ten minutes after the next run to compare observations, including what had worked well.
followUps: What prevented the team from reflecting before that change?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Experience alone does not guarantee learning; successful work also deserves examination.

reading: The reflecting stage of the experiential learning cycle is where teams carefully and critically consider something. Teams reflect on their experience to find ways to solve problems, improve performance, and innovate new ideas. Teams that cannot move from reflecting to deciding are not learning.
example: For example, a team may struggle to reflect on their experience for several reasons. If there is a lack of psychological safety, team members may hesitate to speak honestly about mistakes or challenges. Poor facilitation can cause reflection sessions to become unfocused or dominated by a few voices, limiting meaningful discussion. In a blame-oriented culture, reflection may devolve into finger-pointing rather than collaborative problem-solving. Time pressure and focusing on immediate tasks can make reflection seem like a low priority.

Additionally, unresolved conflict or low trust among team members can lead to defensiveness and closed-off communication. Without precise data or feedback, the team may not have the information needed to understand what went wrong. Finally, overconfidence or complacency can cause a team to dismiss the need for reflection. These barriers can prevent a team from progressing in the experiential learning cycle.
questions: Does your team routinely reflect on its experience to see if there is anything that the team can learn?
What processes or procedures allow team members to share those observations with others?
Based on your experience, what are some of the challenges that prevent teams from moving from reflecting to deciding? How can those challenges be overcome?

coaching.idea: Reflection should produce understanding that supports a decision.
listenFor: Critical review of evidence and assumptions
A concrete choice emerging from discussion
coaching.sampleResponse: We reviewed a recurring error using actual examples rather than accusations. Once we identified the confusing handoff, we chose a revised check instead of ending with general frustration.
followUps: What did the reflection reveal, and how did it influence the decision?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Reflection is not endless discussion, venting, or assigning blame without examining causes.

reading: The deciding stage of the experiential learning cycle is where teams use experience and reflection to guide their decision-making. Often, teams will need to make timely decisions without optimal information. Improving, innovating, and solving problems require teams to move from deciding to acting. Teams that cannot move from deciding to acting are not learning.
example: For example, a leadership team may struggle to make decisions because they wait for information that may never come. Fear of making the wrong choice can lead to analysis paralysis, where the team becomes stuck in endless data gathering and risk assessment. Sometimes, team members may disagree on the best path forward and avoid making a decision altogether to prevent conflict. Leadership may also lack confidence or authority, causing hesitation to commit to a course of action. Additionally, unclear priorities or shifting organizational goals can make it difficult for the team to align on what matters most. Without the ability to make timely decisions, even in uncertainty, the team cannot move forward – and as a result, they miss opportunities to learn, adapt, and grow.
questions: Is your team effective at making decisions? How can the team improve?
What are some typical excuses for not making a timely decision?
Should leaders always get input from their teams before making decisions? Why or why not?
Based on your experience, what are some of the challenges that prevent teams from moving from deciding to acting? How can those challenges be overcome?

coaching.idea: Deciding requires selecting a course of action with imperfect information.
listenFor: An explicit choice made in time
coaching.sampleResponse: We had two workable staffing options and incomplete demand data. We compared risks, chose one by the deadline, and set a review point rather than collecting data indefinitely.
followUps: What uncertainty remained, and why was deciding still reasonable?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: More data is not always better if delay prevents useful action.

reading: The acting stage of the experiential learning cycle is where teams act to further a decision. Good teams will have a bias for action, which favors action over inaction, especially in the face of uncertainty. Improving, innovating, and solving problems require teams to complete the learning cycle by moving from acting to a new and improved experience (ideally). Even if the experience is not what the team expected, learning has occurred, and the cycle begins again.
example: For example, a team may agree on a decision to streamline a workflow but fail to act on it due to a lack of clarity around roles and responsibilities. Without clear ownership, no one takes the lead, and momentum is lost. In other cases, limited resources – such as time, budget, or personnel – can prevent the team from implementing the decision effectively. Resistance to change may also play a role, with some team members reverting to old habits despite the agreed-upon direction. Additionally, poor communication can lead to misunderstandings about what action is required or when it should happen. Sometimes, leadership may not provide the necessary support or follow-through to reinforce the decision. When decisions are not put into action, or actions are poorly executed, the learning cycle is interrupted, and the team misses out on valuable insights that only come through doing.
questions: Does your team have a bias for action? How can the team improve?
What are the common excuses for not acting after a decision has been made?

coaching.idea: A decision becomes learning through action and review of the result.
coaching.sampleResponse: We assigned a person and date to pilot the new handoff. The pilot exposed another gap, which we brought back into reflection instead of calling the whole attempt useless.
followUps: Who acted, and what did the next experience teach the team?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Agreeing on a plan is not the same as implementing it; bias for action is not recklessness.

tasks.title: Set Collective Goals for Teams
tasks.what: Teams need clear goals and stretch goals.

reading: Team goals are objectives or targets that a team is trying to reach or achieve together. They should be well-defined and understood by the team. Establishing stretch goals promotes more learning, better performance, and productivity. Stretch goals are purposefully ambitious and challenge a person or team to step outside their comfort zone. Setting stretch goals forces teams to improve, innovate, and solve problems (team learning).
example: For example, a marketing team sets a stretch goal to double their online engagement within three months. As they begin working toward this ambitious target, they quickly realize that their current content strategy and posting schedule are ineffective enough to meet the goal. By setting a stretch goal for the team, they can identify gaps in their approach – such as inconsistent branding and lack of audience targeting – that may have gone unnoticed. This clarity allows them to brainstorm new strategies, experiment with fresh ideas, and adapt their efforts in real time. In this way, the stretch goal not only pushes performance but also drives valuable learning through problem identification and solution-seeking.
questions: Have performance and learning goals been established for your team?
Do you believe that everyone on the team understands the team goals?
Does your team establish stretch goals? If not, why not?

coaching.idea: Clear shared goals and appropriate stretch goals stimulate team learning.
coaching.sampleResponse: We aimed to reduce turnaround while maintaining quality. Because the target exceeded our usual performance, the team tested a new handoff rather than simply working longer hours.
followUps: What did the stretch goal make the team learn or change?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Stretch goals should challenge methods, not normalize impossible demands or sacrificed standards.

reading: Setting collective goals for teams requires unity of effort, which is the deliberate coordination and cooperation of people toward a common objective. Cohesive teams working in a positive climate are more likely to demonstrate unity of effort.
example: For example, a software development team is tasked with launching a new application feature within a tight deadline. Because the team is cohesive and works in a positive climate, members openly communicate, support one another, and stay focused on the shared goal. The developers, designers, and testers coordinate their efforts closely, adjusting their workflows to avoid delays and quickly resolve issues as they arise. The team pulls together rather than pointing fingers when unexpected challenges occur, such as a critical bug or shifting client requirements. Their unity of effort ensures steady progress and ultimately leads to a successful launch. Without that shared commitment and collaboration, the team would struggle to stay aligned and meet their objective.
questions: Once goals are established, does your team have unity of effort toward that common objective?

coaching.idea: Unity of effort means deliberate coordination toward a common objective.
coaching.sampleResponse: Sales and operations had separate targets that caused rushed promises. We agreed on a shared delivery objective and reviewed capacity together before making commitments.
followUps: Where had the team's efforts been working against each other?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Unity of effort is more than everyone being busy or agreeing that teamwork is important.

reading: Setting collective goals for teams also requires that leaders explain the “why” for the goal. Leaders explain “why” something needs to be accomplished so that teams can develop or adapt their plans for “how” to get the work done.
example: For example, a team is assigned to reduce customer complaints about product delivery delays. Instead of simply directing the team to “fix the delivery issue,” the leader explains the “why” behind the task: to improve the overall customer experience and protect the company’s reputation. By understanding “why” the work matters, the team is better equipped to develop creative and flexible solutions for “how” to address the problem. They explore options such as optimizing shipping routes, adjusting inventory levels, and improving customer communication. When new challenges arise, the team can adapt their plans without waiting for further instructions because they clearly understand the “why” behind their efforts. Explaining why gives direction without micromanaging, enabling teams to stay aligned and agile.
questions: Have you worked for someone who is especially good or bad at explaining “why” something that needs to be accomplished? How did that affect the team’s ability to get the job done?
Is your team good at using “why” as guidance to develop plans? Could they improve?

coaching.idea: Explaining why lets teams adapt how they achieve a goal.
listenFor: Methods adjusted without losing that purpose
coaching.sampleResponse: I explained that the goal was fewer customer interruptions, not just faster calls. The team changed its follow-up process instead of cutting conversations short to meet a speed metric.
followUps: Could team members explain the purpose well enough to choose a different method?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Explaining why is not dictating every step or relying on a slogan without practical meaning.

reading: Establishing incremental goals helps teams develop confidence. An incremental goal is a benchmark set between a starting point and an end goal that is used to track progress. Meeting incremental goals creates short-term wins and provides motivation.
example: For example, a sales team sets a year-end goal to increase revenue by 25%. To stay on track and build momentum, the team establishes incremental monthly targets. Each time they meet a monthly goal, they celebrate the progress, reflect on what worked, and adjust their strategies as needed. These short-term wins improve team morale and reinforce their belief that the larger goal is achievable. Even in months where they fall slightly short, the incremental goals provide a clear sense of direction and help the team stay focused and motivated. Over time, this steady progress builds confidence and strengthens the team’s ability to reach ambitious objectives.
questions: Does your team establish incremental goals? If so, are they helpful? If not, why not?

coaching.idea: Incremental goals create visible progress and confidence.
coaching.sampleResponse: We divided a difficult rollout into a small pilot, one department, and then expansion. Each milestone showed what needed correction and gave the team a credible short-term win.
followUps: How did the milestone tell you whether the team was actually closer to the goal?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Checking off easy tasks is not useful progress if they do not advance the final outcome.

reading: As teams accomplish goals together, they develop higher levels of collective efficacy. Teams that are higher in collective efficacy are better prepared to overcome adversity.
example: For example, a project team tasked with implementing a new company-wide software system faces several early setbacks, including technical issues and resistance from end users. However, because the team has completed challenging projects together, they remain confident in figuring things out. Instead of getting discouraged, they draw on their shared experience, collaborate effectively under pressure, and adjust their approach as needed. Their belief in one another’s capabilities—built through past goal achievement—helps them push through the obstacles and ultimately deliver a successful rollout. This strong sense of collective efficacy enables the team to stay resilient and solution-focused, even amid uncertainty and adversity.
questions: Has the collective efficacy of your team improved over time because of accomplishing goals?
Based on your experience, what are some other challenges and best practices for setting collective goals for teams?

coaching.idea: Achieving goals together strengthens belief in joint capability.
listenFor: How that experience influences the next challenge
coaching.sampleResponse: After the team completed a difficult rollout together, members volunteered ideas for the next one. They could point to specific coordination skills that had worked, not just hope.
followUps: What evidence from the earlier goal supports confidence about the next challenge?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Collective efficacy is grounded in capability and learning, not a guarantee of future success.

tasks.title: Encourage Constructive Dialogue
tasks.what: Honest, safe discussion that surfaces better answers.

reading: Constructive dialogue is essential for teams to improve, innovate, and solve problems (team learning). Constructive dialogue is how teams progress through the experiential learning cycle together. Constructive dialogue is a psychologically safe discussion between people of varying opinions and perspectives that seeks to develop understanding about important and complicated issues.
example: For example, a cross-functional team holds a debrief to understand what went wrong after a product launch falls short of expectations. During the discussion, team members from marketing, design, and engineering openly share their perspectives on what contributed to the outcome. Instead of assigning blame, they listen actively, ask clarifying questions, and build on each other’s insights. One team member points out communication gaps, while another highlights how customer feedback wasn’t fully integrated into the final product. Because the environment is psychologically safe, everyone feels comfortable speaking up, even when their viewpoints differ. This constructive dialogue allows the team to make sense of the experience together, identify meaningful lessons, and agree on improvements—moving them forward in the experiential learning cycle.
questions: Is your team able to engage in constructive dialogue? If not, why not?

coaching.idea: Constructive dialogue brings different perspectives into a safe search for understanding.
coaching.sampleResponse: Two colleagues disagreed about the cause of delays. We compared their evidence and asked clarifying questions until both saw a handoff gap neither could identify alone.
followUps: What changed in the team's understanding because different views were heard?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Constructive dialogue is not winning a debate or requiring everyone to agree.

reading: Psychological safety is the feeling or belief that you can share thoughts, opinions, and ideas freely without fear of damaging your reputation or standing. Trust and mutual respect are the foundations of psychological safety.
example: For example, during a team meeting to review a failed marketing campaign, a junior team member suggests that the campaign messaging may have missed the mark with the target audience. Rather than dismissing or criticizing the comment, the team leader thanks them for their honesty and invites others to share their thoughts. More team members begin to contribute, offering different perspectives and insights that hadn’t been considered before. Because the team has built trust and mutual respect over time, members feel safe to voice concerns, admit mistakes, and challenge ideas without fear of embarrassment or backlash. This psychological safety creates an open environment where real learning and improvement occur.
questions: How would you rate the psychological safety of your team? Could it be improved?
Do you personally feel psychologically safe at work? If not, why not?
How does creating a positive climate and developing cohesion promote psychological safety?

coaching.idea: Psychological safety enables people to speak honestly without fear of humiliation.
listenFor: A leader's response to uncomfortable input
Evidence that people can raise mistakes or concerns
coaching.sampleResponse: A junior colleague flagged an error in my plan. I thanked them, checked the issue, and corrected it publicly. Others then raised concerns earlier rather than waiting silently.
followUps: How do you react when the message is inconvenient or challenges your authority?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Psychological safety does not mean lowering standards or avoiding difficult feedback.

reading: Psychological safety promotes adaptive thinking. Adaptive thinking is recognizing unexpected situations, quickly considering various possible responses, and making an appropriate decision.
example: For example, during a live product demo with a major client, a technical glitch causes a key feature to stop working. Instead of panicking or freezing, a team member quickly suggests a workaround using a different tool. Another teammate jumps in to adjust the presentation flow while someone else troubleshoots. Because the team operates in a psychologically safe environment, they’re comfortable thinking on their feet, sharing ideas without hesitation, and taking quick action without fear of being judged for making a mistake. Their ability to adapt in the moment keeps the demo on track and impresses the client with their professionalism and teamwork.
questions: How would you rate yourself on adaptive thinking?
Is your team good at adaptive thinking together?

coaching.idea: Safe communication supports adaptive thinking when circumstances change.
coaching.sampleResponse: A teammate noticed the planned route was blocked and felt safe to interrupt the briefing. We quickly compared alternatives and redirected the team before committing more resources.
followUps: How did the ability to speak up affect the speed or quality of adaptation?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Adaptive thinking is a reasoned adjustment, not changing direction randomly.

tasks.title: Build New Mental Models
tasks.what: Mental Models = “How we do things around here.”
tasks.why: Teams must adapt mental models to improve and embrace change.

reading: Watch this video (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RMUO-Eol1NQ)

As teams work together over time, they develop shared mental models built on experience and training. A mental model is “how we do things around here.” Shared mental models improve team performance by enabling team members to accurately describe, predict, and explain the team’s expected behaviors and actions.
example: For example, an emergency response team has trained and worked together through multiple real-world incidents. When a new situation arises – such as a sudden equipment failure during a rescue – they don’t need to stop and explain every step. Each member instinctively understands their role, anticipates the actions of others, and adapts in real time based on a shared understanding of the team’s procedures and priorities. Because they’ve developed shared mental models through experience and training, they can coordinate efficiently under pressure, make faster decisions, and maintain high performance even in unpredictable environments. This collective mindset enhances their ability to respond effectively and cohesively as a unit.
questions: How important are shared mental models in your line of work?
Does your team share mental models about how to do things together in the workplace?
Would you describe your team as being “on the same page” most of the time at work?
In your experience, how do shared mental models help teams solve problems and overcome challenges? Explain.

coaching.idea: Mental models are shared expectations about how the team works.
listenFor: An unwritten or explicit operating assumption
coaching.sampleResponse: On our crew, whoever discovered a fault contacted the next shift directly. That shared expectation let others predict the handoff instead of assuming a supervisor would handle it.
followUps: What does your team take for granted about how work gets done?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: A mental model is broader than a written checklist; unstated assumptions matter too.

reading: Shared mental models are not identical. Instead, they are compatible and complementary. Shared mental models enable better coordination, cooperation, and communication. Shared mental models enhance the team’s ability to solve problems, improve, and innovate. Teams that share mental models make better collective decisions.
example: For example, a product development team is preparing to launch a new feature. The designers, engineers, and marketers have different areas of expertise, but they share a common understanding of the project’s goals, user needs, and timeline. While their individual mental models reflect their specific roles, these models are compatible and complementary – each team member knows how their work fits into the bigger picture. As a result, they can anticipate each other’s needs, coordinate tasks more effectively, and quickly adapt when unexpected issues arise. When a last-minute technical challenge threatens the launch, the team collaborates seamlessly to find a solution, drawing on their shared understanding to make a fast, informed decision. This alignment enables them to solve problems creatively and keep the project on track.
questions: Has your team’s ability to coordinate, cooperate, and communicate improved over time?
Is your team more effective and efficient because of shared mental models?
In your experience, how important are shared mental models during adversity? Explain.

coaching.idea: Shared models need to be compatible, not identical.
listenFor: Different role perspectives that fit together
coaching.sampleResponse: The dispatcher tracked routes while technicians tracked repairs. They used different details but agreed on what ready meant, so neither scheduled work before the other could support it.
followUps: Which expectations must align, even if each role sees the work differently?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Shared mental models do not require identical knowledge or the elimination of different perspectives.

reading: As teams improve, innovate, and solve problems (team learning), it creates change in the workplace. Change in the workplace always requires people and teams to build new mental models. In a dynamic environment where change is constant, people must routinely adapt to new plans, policies, processes, and procedures. When mental models are entrenched (not a bad thing), change is usually resisted.
example: For example, a company shifts from a traditional in-office work model to a hybrid remote structure. While the new model offers flexibility and efficiency, some team members struggle to adapt. They’re used to face-to-face meetings, structured daily routines, and clear boundaries between work and home. Their existing mental models – shaped by years of in-office norms – make embracing the new working method challenging. Despite training and new communication tools, some employees resist the change, feeling disconnected or unsure how to collaborate effectively in a virtual environment. This resistance isn’t due to unwillingness, but rather the challenge of reshaping deeply ingrained expectations and behaviors. Building new mental models takes time, experience, and support, but it’s essential for teams to thrive in evolving circumstances.
questions: Have you ever heard... “That’s not how we do it here” or “That will never work here” in the workplace?
How would you rate yourself at embracing change in the workplace?
How would you rate your team at embracing change in the workplace?

coaching.idea: Workplace change often requires changing familiar expectations and routines.
listenFor: Practice building a workable new model
coaching.sampleResponse: A new booking system shifted who confirmed appointments. We discussed the old expectation, clarified the new owner, and practiced handoffs until people stopped relying on the previous routine.
followUps: What assumption was behind the resistance, and what helped people replace it?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Resistance may reflect a well-established model, not simply a bad attitude.

reading: Single-loop learning is problem-solving by changing strategies and techniques to avoid mistakes and improve efficiency in existing systems. In single-loop learning, mental models do not change, and decision-making rules remain the same.
example: For example, a customer support team notices that response times are slower than desired. To fix the issue, they adjusted their internal workflow by assigning tickets based on urgency rather than arrival time. This change leads to faster resolution for high-priority issues and improves customer satisfaction. However, the team doesn’t question or change their broader assumptions about how support is delivered or why specific issues arise in the first place. They are improving performance within the existing system, using the same goals and decision-making rules. This is single-loop learning – enhancing efficiency without challenging the underlying mental models or questioning whether the system needs to change.
questions: What problem did your team recently solve that required single-loop learning?

coaching.idea: Single-loop learning improves methods within existing assumptions.
listenFor: An underlying rule that stays unchanged
coaching.sampleResponse: We kept our same approval requirement but added reminders to reduce delays. The process improved, although we never questioned whether every request needed approval.
followUps: Which decision rule stayed the same after the change?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: A faster or better process is not automatically a new mental model.

reading: Double-loop learning is about surfacing, challenging, and ultimately building new mental models. In double-loop learning, mental models do change and so the rules for making decisions must also change.
example: For example, a quality assurance team regularly deals with product defects late in the production process. At first, they try to improve inspection procedures and tighten quality checks – classic single- loop learning. However, when the problems persist, they step back and question their core assumptions about quality control. Through discussion and analysis, they realize that waiting until the end of production to inspect for defects is reactive and inefficient. This leads them to adopt a new mental model: building quality into the process from the start. They shift to a proactive approach, involving QA in the early stages of design and development and empowering all team members to take ownership of quality. This fundamental change in thinking and practice is double-loop learning – where improving outcomes requires rethinking actions and the beliefs and assumptions that drive them.
questions: What problem did your team recently solve that required double-loop learning?
In your experience, is double-loop learning more difficult?

coaching.idea: Double-loop learning challenges assumptions and changes decision rules.
listenFor: A resulting change to how decisions are made
coaching.sampleResponse: We questioned the belief that every routine request required a manager's signature. After reviewing the risks, we authorized staff to decide low-risk cases within clear limits.
followUps: What belief or rule changed, beyond making the existing process faster?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: A large or expensive improvement is not necessarily double-loop learning.

reading: Change is not always about fixing something that is broken. Often, change is about taking something good and making it even better. Change is inevitable, especially when teams are constantly improving, innovating, and problem-solving (team learning).
example: For example, a high-performing sales team consistently meets its quarterly targets and has a strong track record of success. While nothing appears to be broken, leadership sees an opportunity to improve by adopting a new customer relationship management (CRM) system that offers better analytics and automation. Some team members are hesitant, believing the current system works just fine. However, after training and hands-on use, they see how the new CRM can streamline their workflow, provide deeper insights into customer behavior, and help them close deals more efficiently. In this case, change isn’t about fixing failure – it’s about enhancing what already works to unlock even greater performance and potential.
questions: Have you ever heard... “If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it” in the workplace?
Based on your experience, why do you think change is often resisted in the workplace?
Based on your experience, what are some other challenges and best practices for building new mental models?

coaching.idea: Even successful ways of working can benefit from change.
listenFor: A reason to improve something already working
Support for adopting the better approach
coaching.sampleResponse: Our handoffs met the standard, but customers still repeated information. We tested a shared record to improve their experience and helped the team learn the new routine.
followUps: What made the change worthwhile even though the old method was not failing?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Change should have a purpose; constant change without a learning goal is not improvement.

modules.title: Organizational Learning
modules.theme: Organizations that learn and change faster than their competition stay ahead. Vision aligns it; knowledge creation and sharing power it.
glossary: Moving the whole organization to a new way
What the organization wants to become
The shared values that support or block change
The current way — what change has to overcome
A group that learns a craft together

tasks.title: Analyze Organizational Learning Capacity
tasks.what: Organizational learning is the ability to continuously improve and innovate to gain or maintain competitive advantage.
tasks.why: Organizations that learn and change faster than others are more adaptive, resilient, and effective.

reading: Organizational learning involves continuously improving and innovating to gain and maintain a competitive advantage. Learning organizations must be skilled at both continuous improvement and innovation. Improvement, innovation, and problem-solving (team learning) at the team level is the foundation of organizational learning.
example: For example, a product development team regularly holds retrospectives after each project sprint to identify what went well and could be improved. Over time, these reflections lead to small but meaningful process changes, such as better communication between designers and engineers or more realistic sprint planning. At the same time, the team is encouraged to experiment with bold new ideas, like testing emerging technologies or rethinking the user experience from the ground up. These efforts not only improve current performance but also spark innovation. As the team’s learning compounds, their successes and insights influence other teams across the organization. What starts as local improvement grows into a culture of learning that drives the entire company forward, giving it a lasting competitive edge.
questions: How would you rate your organization’s capacity to learn?

coaching.idea: Organizational learning builds on team learning and spreads improvement and innovation.
listenFor: A link from local learning to wider practice
coaching.sampleResponse: One branch tested a better intake process. We reviewed its results, adapted it with other branches, and updated training so the improvement became usable across the organization.
followUps: How did the organization learn, rather than just one successful team?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: An isolated local improvement is not enough evidence that the whole organization learns effectively.

reading: Continuous improvement refers to improving a product, service, or process. Innovation refers to creating a new product, service, or process.
example: For example, a customer service team analyzes call data and realizes customers are frequently confused about billing. To address this, they revise their training materials and update their call scripts to provide more straightforward explanations – this is continuous improvement, as they’re enhancing an existing process. At the same time, another team proposes developing a self-service billing chatbot that allows customers to get instant answers without speaking to an agent. Since this is a new way to deliver service, it represents innovation. Both efforts contribute to better customer experiences, but they approach the goal from different angles – one by refining what already exists and the other by creating something entirely new.
questions: Have you or your team made a product, service, or process better recently?
Have you or your team created a new product, service, or process recently?

coaching.idea: Continuous improvement refines existing work; innovation creates something new.
coaching.sampleResponse: We improved our existing booking process by removing duplicate entry. Separately, we created a remote consultation service that we had never offered before.
followUps: What already existed in the improvement example, and what was new in the innovation example?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Calling every small adjustment innovation hides the difference between refining and creating.

reading: Competitive advantage puts an organization in a favorable position compared to competitors. The surest way for an organization to gain and maintain a competitive advantage is to learn and change faster than the competition.
example: For example, a tech company closely monitors user feedback and market trends to adapt its product offerings quickly. When a new competitor releases a popular feature, the company’s teams rapidly gather insights, adjust their development priorities, and launch an improved version within weeks. At the same time, they experiment with emerging technologies and invest in employee learning to stay ahead of industry shifts. Because the organization has built a culture of continuous learning and agile decision-making, it can respond to changes in the market faster than competitors. This ability to learn and change quickly allows the company to stay relevant, meet customer needs more effectively, and maintain a strong competitive advantage.
questions: Why is competitive advantage important to a for-profit organization?
Why is competitive advantage important to a non-profit organization?
Is competitive advantage important to a government organization?
Is competitive advantage more critical to some government organizations than others? Explain.
Does your organization have a competitive advantage? If so, what is it, and how was it developed?

coaching.idea: Learning and adapting can strengthen an organization's relative effectiveness.
listenFor: What advantage means in that setting
coaching.sampleResponse: Our service organization learned from response data and redesigned coverage faster than comparable providers. For us, advantage meant more reliable access for the people we served, not just profit.
followUps: Who are you comparing with, and what useful outcome defines advantage?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Competitive advantage should be explained in context rather than assumed to mean sales or profit everywhere.

reading: Organizational change is the transition of an organization from its current state to some desired future state. For an organization to change, it must be willing and able to learn. Change is not possible without learning.
example: For example, a healthcare organization transitions from paper-based patient records to a fully digital system. This change requires more than just new software – it demands new skills, workflows, and mindsets. Staff must be trained not only on how to use the technology but also on how to think differently about data management and patient care. At first, there is resistance, as some employees are uncomfortable with the unfamiliar tools. However, the organization begins to learn together through ongoing training, support, and constructive dialogue. As people become more confident and adapt their practices, the organization moves closer to its desired future state. This transformation illustrates that meaningful change depends on a shared willingness and ability to learn at every level.
questions: How would you rate your organization’s capacity to change?
Does your organization have positions dedicated to change management? If so, are they effective at what they do?

coaching.idea: Organizational change requires people and teams to learn new ways of working.
listenFor: New skills and assumptions needed to reach it
coaching.sampleResponse: We moved to digital records, but software alone did not change the work. Teams practiced new handoffs, clarified ownership, and used feedback to correct the rollout.
followUps: What learning was necessary beyond announcing the change or installing the tool?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: A new policy or system is not proof that people have learned to work differently.

tasks.title: Promote a Shared Vision
tasks.what: Vision describes what the organization wants to become in the future.
tasks.why: A clear vision aligns people and teams, drives learning, and creates motivation for change.

reading: Vision describes what an organization wants to be in the future. A bold and aspirational vision will drive learning and change in an organization.
example: For example, a renewable energy company has a clear mission to design and install solar power systems for homes and businesses. This guides their daily operations and short-term goals. However, their vision – to become the leading provider of clean, affordable energy worldwide – pushes them to think bigger and constantly evolve. To realize this vision, the organization invests in new technologies, expands into emerging markets, and encourages employees to experiment with innovative solutions. Even though their current mission is being fulfilled, the bold and aspirational vision drives continuous learning, strategic risk-taking, and long-term change that sets them apart from competitors and brings them closer to achieving their future state.
questions: Has your organization published a mission and/or vision statement on its website?
Does your organization’s vision statement describe a future that it is trying to achieve?

coaching.idea: Vision describes a meaningful future that can motivate learning and change.
coaching.sampleResponse: Our vision was to make service accessible without unnecessary travel. That gave teams a reason to learn remote support methods instead of just processing today's requests faster.
followUps: What future does the vision describe, and what must the organization learn to reach it?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Vision is not simply a daily task list or a numerical target without direction.

reading: Promoting a shared vision helps align the efforts of people and teams across the organization and keeps them headed in the same direction.
example: For example, a global logistics company introduces a shared vision of becoming the most reliable and sustainable delivery service in the industry. This vision is communicated clearly and consistently across all departments – from warehouse operations to customer service and technology teams. As a result, teams begin to align their goals and efforts with the broader organizational vision. The operations team looks for ways to reduce emissions in transportation, the IT team develops more efficient tracking systems, and customer service emphasizes transparency and trust. Even though each team has different responsibilities, the shared vision keeps everyone moving in the same direction, fostering unity, collaboration, and purpose throughout the organization.
questions: Do you and your team have a good understanding of your organization’s vision?
How does the organization’s vision affect what you and your team do day-to-day to accomplish goals and objectives?

coaching.idea: A shared vision aligns decisions across teams.
coaching.sampleResponse: When departments proposed competing projects, we assessed which best supported accessible service. Different teams chose different actions, but their priorities contributed to the same future.
followUps: How did the vision help resolve a real conflict between priorities?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Repeating the same statement does not prove teams are making aligned decisions.

reading: Organizations are better at learning and change when people believe in their purpose and “buy into” their vision. Leaders’ daily actions, especially senior leaders’, must be consistent with the organization’s vision.
example: For example, a technology company has a bold vision to make digital tools more accessible to underserved communities worldwide. The CEO regularly communicates the purpose behind this vision – bridging the digital divide and empowering people through technology. Instead of focusing solely on profit, senior leaders invest in outreach programs, develop low-cost product options, and partner with nonprofits to expand access. Employees see leaders prioritizing social impact in decision-making and resource allocation, which builds trust and belief in the vision. As a result, teams across the company – from engineers to marketers – are motivated to innovate with inclusivity in mind. This shared purpose helps align efforts and accelerates organizational learning and change.
questions: What is the purpose that drives your organization toward its vision?
Do you believe in your organization’s purpose and vision?
Are you able to promote the organization’s vision? If not, why not?
Are the actions of senior leaders in your organization consistent with the organization’s vision?
Do senior leaders believe in the organization’s purpose and vision?

coaching.idea: People believe a vision when leaders' actions support it.
listenFor: Visible consistency between words and decisions
coaching.sampleResponse: We said learning mattered, so I protected time for a pilot even during a busy period. Cutting every learning activity while praising innovation would have sent the opposite message.
followUps: What decision showed that the vision mattered when it carried a cost?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: A persuasive launch speech cannot overcome repeated contradictory actions.

reading: Organizations realize their visions by building a great culture and executing a sound strategy. Culture is the shared assumptions, values, and beliefs that govern how people behave across the organization.
example: For example, a financial services company has a vision to become the most trusted advisor in the industry. To achieve this, they focus on building a culture of integrity, transparency, and client-first thinking. These values are reinforced through hiring practices, leadership behavior, recognition programs, and daily decision-making. The company also embraces a culture of learning and change, encouraging employees to seek feedback, pursue professional development, and experiment with new ideas. Continuous improvement and innovation are seen as shared responsibilities, not isolated efforts.
questions: How would you describe the culture of your organization? What do the people in your organization collectively value and believe in?
Does the culture in your organization help or hinder the execution of strategy? Explain.
Does the culture in your organization help or hinder learning and change? Explain.

coaching.idea: Culture and strategy work together to turn a vision into reality.
listenFor: Plans that those behaviors support or undermine
coaching.sampleResponse: We planned to improve service through experimentation, but people feared admitting mistakes. We changed how reviews were handled so honest learning could support the strategy.
followUps: Which cultural behavior was helping or blocking execution?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: A strategy document cannot by itself change the assumptions that govern daily behavior.

reading: Culture sets the conditions for an effective strategy, which is a roadmap of plans and policies for accomplishing an organization’s long-term goals and objectives .
example: For example, a healthcare organization develops a strategy to expand its services into rural communities using mobile clinics and telehealth technology. The strategy is clear and well-researched, but its success depends heavily on the organization’s culture. Because the organization has a culture that values collaboration, innovation, and community engagement, staff are willing to embrace new roles, adapt to unfamiliar environments, and work closely with local partners. Employees are encouraged to share feedback from the field, which leads to real-time improvements in the implementation of the strategy. Without a culture that supports flexibility, learning, and mission-driven work, even the best strategy could stall. In this case, culture sets the conditions that allow the strategy to take root and produce meaningful, long-term results.
questions: Are you and your team confident that your organization’s strategy for reaching long-term goals and objectives is working? If not, why not?
How does learning support an organization’s ability to execute strategy?

coaching.idea: Strategy is a roadmap; culture affects whether people can execute it.
listenFor: A long-term goal and coordinated plans
Cultural conditions that enable the plans
coaching.sampleResponse: Our expansion plan required departments to share resources. We reinforced collaboration in leadership decisions because rewarding only local wins kept undermining the roadmap.
followUps: What plan or policy connects today's work to the long-term goal?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Strategy is more than a vision statement or a collection of disconnected projects.

reading: The plans and policies developed to achieve long-term goals and objectives (strategy) are more likely to succeed when the organization’s people collectively value learning and believe that change is possible (culture).
example: For example, a retail organization develops a strategy to transition from primarily in-store sales to a more robust e-commerce model over the next five years. This shift requires significant changes in technology, logistics, and customer engagement. The strategy is bold, but it’s more likely to succeed because the organization has a culture where people value learning and believe that change is necessary and achievable. Store associates are eager to cross-train in digital customer service, managers embrace new data tools to make better decisions, and teams openly share lessons learned during pilot programs. Rather than resisting the shift, employees lean into the challenge because the culture supports adaptability, growth, and shared ownership of success. This collective mindset enables the organization to implement its strategy effectively and remain competitive in a rapidly evolving market.
questions: Do the people in your organization value learning? If not, why not?
Do you and your team value learning? If so, how is that value expressed at work?
Does your organization have policies that support a culture of learning? What are some examples of those policies?
Do people believe that change is possible in your organization? If not, why not?
Do you and your team believe that change is possible in your organization? If not, why not?

coaching.idea: A culture that values learning makes change-oriented strategy more workable.
listenFor: Routine support for testing and learning
coaching.sampleResponse: Before a major process change, teams ran small experiments and shared lessons without blame. Those habits made the wider rollout more credible and easier to adjust.
followUps: What everyday behavior shows people value learning rather than merely say they do?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: A positive attitude alone does not execute strategy; people also need capability, resources, and action.

tasks.title: Foster Knowledge Creation
tasks.what: Knowledge creation is the continuous generation of new ideas that improve, innovate, or solve problems.
tasks.why: Frontline workers and supervisors often have the best ideas because they are closest to the work.

reading: Knowledge creation in an organization is the deliberate and continuous process of generating new ideas that lead to improvements, innovations, and problem-solving. The frontline supervisors and teams who interact the most with the organization’s products, services, and customers are often the best source of new ideas.
example: For example, in a manufacturing company, workers on the assembly line notice that a specific machine frequently jams during a particular part of the production process. Rather than simply reporting the issue, the team experiments with a slight adjustment to the material feed that significantly reduces the number of jams. The supervisor observes the improvement and encourages the team to document their findings. Once shared with engineering and leadership, the adjustment is tested more broadly and adopted across multiple production lines. This small but impactful change leads to increased efficiency and less downtime. Because the organization values the insights of those closest to the work, new knowledge is continuously created and applied, fueling improvement and innovation.
questions: Does your organization recognize the ideas of frontline supervisors and their teams? If so, is there room for improvement?

coaching.idea: New organizational knowledge often starts with frontline observations and ideas.
listenFor: Deliberate development into a useful idea
coaching.sampleResponse: A frontline colleague noticed customers repeatedly misunderstood one instruction. We investigated the pattern and tested a revised explanation instead of dismissing it as isolated complaints.
followUps: How did an observation become a tested idea the organization could use?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: An idea is a starting point; usefulness needs exploration rather than automatic adoption.

reading: Learning organizations recognize new knowledge at the team level and then codify it into organizational plans, policies, processes, or procedures.
example: For example, a customer support team notices a recurring issue with a popular product that is not addressed in the current troubleshooting guide. Through experience and collaboration, the team develops a faster, more effective solution. Initially, this new knowledge existed only at the team level and was shared informally among a few members. However, once the team brings the solution to management and it’s reviewed and validated, the organization updates the official support documentation and training materials. The solution is also added to the onboarding process for new hires. At this point, the knowledge has fully emerged and become part of the organization’s formal processes – transforming individual learning into organizational learning.
questions: Once new knowledge is created in your organization, what are the obstacles to recognizing that knowledge?
What are the obstacles to integrating that new knowledge into practice?

coaching.idea: Codifying learning turns a local insight into a repeatable organizational practice.
listenFor: Incorporation into guidance, training, or procedures
coaching.sampleResponse: A team tested a better equipment check and documented when it worked. We updated the procedure and training, named an owner, and reviewed whether other locations achieved similar results.
followUps: Where is the learning recorded, and how will it stay current?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Saving a document does not ensure that the practice is adopted, understood, or maintained.

reading: Leaders at all levels in an organization should encourage and reward creativity. Leaders sometimes dismiss new ideas because they still need work. Instead, leaders should get involved and help develop these ideas into something actionable, if possible.
example: For example, a junior employee in a logistics company proposes using a mobile app to track delivery vehicle maintenance in real time. The idea is rough and lacks technical details, so at first, it’s easy to dismiss it as impractical. However, instead of shutting it down, the team leader sees potential and invites the employee to present the concept at the next planning meeting. With input from IT and operations, the idea is refined into a feasible pilot project. Over time, the app evolved into a valuable tool that reduces breakdowns and improves delivery reliability. By encouraging creativity and actively supporting idea development, the leader not only helps improve operations but also empowers employees to contribute meaningfully to innovation.
questions: How would you rate yourself at welcoming new ideas? Could you improve?
Has one of your ideas, or the idea of a team member, been dismissed because it was only “half-baked”?

coaching.idea: Leaders should help promising unfinished ideas become actionable.
listenFor: A practical test of the idea
coaching.sampleResponse: A colleague suggested a rough scheduling change. Instead of rejecting the gaps, I helped define a small pilot and success measures so we could learn whether the idea was useful.
followUps: What support turned the initial suggestion into something testable?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Encouraging creativity does not mean every proposal must be implemented or praised without scrutiny.

reading: Leaders can foster knowledge creation by challenging the status quo. Status quo is the current or present condition; it is the way things usually are. Leaders should ask themselves and their teams, “Is this actually working?” and “Is this the best we can do?” Constructive dialogue is essential for challenging the status quo.
example: For example, in a hospital setting, a department has followed the same patient discharge procedure for years. While it meets basic requirements, patients often leave confused about follow-up care. A new department head asks tough questions like, “Is this working for our patients?” and “Is this the best we can do?” These questions spark constructive dialogue among nurses, doctors, and administrative staff. The team identifies communication gaps through open discussion and proposes a new, more patient-friendly discharge checklist. The team generates new knowledge about what works better as the revised process is tested and refined. By challenging the status quo and creating space for dialogue, the leader helps surface practical improvements that enhance patient care and drive meaningful organizational learning.
questions: Are you comfortable challenging the status quo at work? If not, why not?
Are people on your team comfortable speaking up when something is not working?
Have you worked for someone who is uncomfortable with challenging the status quo? How did that affect the team?

coaching.idea: Challenge the status quo by examining whether familiar practices still work.
coaching.sampleResponse: We had always required a weekly report nobody used. I asked who relied on it and what decisions it informed; we tested a simpler update based on the actual need.
followUps: What evidence would justify keeping the current practice?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Challenging the status quo is not dismissing experience or changing things solely because they are old.

tasks.title: Ensure Knowledge Sharing
tasks.what: Knowledge sharing is the deliberate exchange of information, skills, experience, and insights.
tasks.why: If new knowledge stays with one person or team, the organization cannot learn from it.

reading: Knowledge sharing in an organization is the deliberate exchange of information, skills, experiences, and insights among employees, teams, and departments. Sharing knowledge ensures that it becomes a collective resource that benefits the whole organization.
example: For example, a regional sales team develops a new approach to onboarding clients that significantly improves customer retention. The new process includes a series of personalized follow-up calls and a streamlined welcome kit that helps clients feel more supported from day one. As a result, their region sees a noticeable uptick in satisfaction scores and repeat business.
