When senior leaders learn of this success, they don’t let it remain isolated – they facilitate knowledge sharing by having the team document the process, share results in a company-wide meeting, and lead a training session for other regional teams. With leadership support, the improved onboarding approach is adopted across the organization, leading to better outcomes company-wide. This intentional sharing and scaling of knowledge ensures that learning in one area benefits the whole organization.
questions: Once new knowledge emerges in your organization, what are the obstacles to sharing that knowledge locally?
What are the obstacles to transferring that knowledge across organizational boundaries?

coaching.idea: Knowledge becomes a collective resource when others can understand and use it.
listenFor: Evidence of learning or use beyond the originator
coaching.sampleResponse: After solving a recurring fault, our team demonstrated the fix to another shift and watched them try it. Their questions helped us improve the explanation before sharing it more widely.
followUps: How do you know the recipient could apply the knowledge?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Posting information is not the same as successful knowledge transfer.

reading: Knowledge sharing is complex when it requires individuals and teams to build new mental models. Even though the new “way of doing things” has proven effective elsewhere in the organization, leaders should expect resistance to change. When leaders personally endorse new practices, knowledge sharing is more likely.
example: For example, a large consulting firm rolls out a new project management system that has significantly improved efficiency and collaboration in one of its regional offices. However, other offices are slow to adopt it, preferring familiar tools and routines. Even with precise data showing better performance, many team members resist the change because it challenges their established working methods. To support knowledge sharing, senior leaders begin actively using the new system themselves, highlighting its benefits in meetings and sharing their own learning experiences. They publicly recognize teams that adopt the new approach and create space for open dialogue about concerns as leaders model the change and reinforce its value, and skepticism shifts. Gradually, more teams embrace the new system, and the improved practices spread across the organization. This example shows how leadership endorsement helps overcome resistance and accelerates the adoption of new mental models.
questions: Have you heard someone say, “That might work over there, but it will never work here “?

coaching.idea: Adopting others' practices may require new mental models and visible leader support.
listenFor: Support for adapting and trying the new practice
coaching.sampleResponse: Another branch's handoff worked well, but our staff assumed it would not fit. I backed a small local trial, discussed their concerns, and helped adapt the process using evidence.
followUps: What made the resistance understandable, and what helped people reconsider?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: A practice proven elsewhere still needs thoughtful application; endorsement alone does not remove local constraints.

reading: A community of practice is a group of people bound by what they have learned through mutual interest and experience in a particular activity. In the world of work, communities of practice are everywhere, and we all belong to one or more.
example: For example, within a hospital system, a group of emergency room nurses forms an informal community of practice focused on improving patient triage. Though they work in different locations, they regularly connect through virtual meetings and messaging platforms to share case experiences, discuss new triage protocols, and exchange tips for handling high-stress situations. Over time, their shared dialogue leads to better practices, which they bring back to their teams. As their collaboration deepens, they become a trusted resource for training new staff. This community of practice strengthens collective expertise, fosters continuous improvement, and enhances the quality of care across the organization.
questions: Which communities of practice do you belong to at work?
Are you more active in some communities than others? If so, why?

coaching.idea: Communities of practice form around shared work, interest, and experience.
coaching.sampleResponse: Technicians from several locations began meeting to discuss difficult repairs. They brought cases, compared approaches, and kept returning because the exchange helped their everyday work.
followUps: What makes this an ongoing community of practitioners rather than a one-time meeting?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: A distribution list or formal reporting structure alone is not a community of practice.

reading: Communities of practice are especially effective at sharing knowledge because they engage in dialogue across traditional organizational boundaries.
example: For example, in a public school district, a community of practice is formed by middle school science teachers from different schools. Although they all have the same role, they teach in different environments and to diverse student populations. They meet regularly – in person and online – to share lesson plans, classroom management strategies, and ways to engage students in hands-on experiments. One teacher shares a creative approach to teaching the scientific method using local community data, which others adapt to fit their classrooms. Because they all do the same job, the dialogue is rich with practical, experience-based knowledge that’s immediately relevant. This community of practice helps them continually improve their teaching, stay current with curriculum standards, and support one another in navigating common challenges.
questions: Do you routinely communicate with people outside of your department or outside of your organization who do the same type of work as you? If so, how do you communicate with them?
Do you routinely learn about the work that you do from people outside of your department or organization?

coaching.idea: Communities of practice help knowledge cross organizational boundaries.
listenFor: A useful application of another group's experience
coaching.sampleResponse: Supervisors from different departments compared onboarding problems. One borrowed a peer's practice, adapted it, and shared the result back so others could learn from the trial.
followUps: Which boundary did the knowledge cross, and what changed because of it?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: Cross-department attendance does not establish sharing unless useful dialogue and learning occur.

reading: Although communities of practice are primarily informal and self- organizing, they are pretty effective at managing knowledge in organizations. Organizations can influence the development and effectiveness of these communities by providing people with the time and resources they need to actively participate in them.
example: For example, in a consulting firm, a group of junior consultants forms a community of practice to share insights on client engagement and project delivery. Initially, they meet informally over lunch or after work, but participation is inconsistent due to busy schedules. Recognizing the potential value, senior leadership supports the group by formally allocating time during work hours for monthly knowledge- sharing sessions and providing a dedicated virtual space for ongoing collaboration. They also invite experienced consultants to mentor the group and contribute to discussions. With this support, the community becomes more active and impactful – sharing templates, refining best practices, and helping new consultants ramp up more quickly. By investing just a nominal amount of time and resources, the organization boosts the effectiveness of the community and strengthens its overall capacity to manage and transfer knowledge.
questions: Does your organization provide support to communities of practice? If so, how?
How do you participate in communities of practice?
How do the people on your team participate in communities of practice?

coaching.idea: Support communities with time and resources while preserving their usefulness to members.
listenFor: Member-led learning tied to real needs
coaching.sampleResponse: We gave a peer learning group protected meeting time and a shared workspace. Members chose relevant problems, and we asked what support helped rather than turning every meeting into a management report.
followUps: How would you support the community without taking over its agenda?
What did you learn, and what would you repeat or change next time?
coaching.misunderstanding: More management control does not automatically make an informal learning community more effective.
